titleEn: To You, O LORD, I call
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Gm | Dm A | Dm Dm |
intro: Nine verses that break in half at verse 6 and never look back. The first five are a plea from someone whose fear is not defeat but silence, and they end by asking that the wicked be handed exactly what they built. Then, with no transition and no account of a rescue, the verbs move to the perfect and the psalm is thanksgiving: He has heard. The word to follow is the one for pleas in verse 2, which comes back whole in verse 6. It is the only phrase repeated across the break, and it is the psalm's own signal that the second half is an answer to the first.

stichs.en: Of David.
To You, O LORD, I call; my rock,
do not be deaf to me,
lest You stay silent toward me
and I become like those who go down to the pit.

verses.summary: Everything is laid out in one verse: the address, the name chosen for God, and the exact fear. Not being refused, being met with nothing.

stichs.en: Hear the voice of my pleas when I cry out to You,
when I lift my hands toward the inner room of Your holiness.

verses.summary: The plea becomes physical. Hands go up toward the innermost room of the sanctuary, which is the direction the answer is expected to come from.

stichs.en: Do not drag me off with the wicked,
or with the doers of iniquity,
who speak peace with their neighbours
while evil is in their heart.

verses.summary: A request not to share a fate. The wicked are defined by a gap between what they say and what they hold, which is the same gap the speaker fears in a silent God.

stichs.en: Give them according to their deed,
and according to the evil of their doings;
as the work of their hands, give to them;
turn back on them what they have earned.

glosses: and according to the evil of
verses.summary: The hardest verse in the psalm to say out loud. Four clauses all ask for one thing: that what their hands made be handed back to them, no more.

stichs.en: For they give no thought to the works of the LORD,
nor to the work of His hands.
He will tear them down and not build them up.

verses.summary: The reason, given late. Their fault is failing to notice what God's hands do, and the charge is built from the same phrase used against their own hands one verse earlier.

stichs.en: Blessed is the LORD,
for He has heard the voice of my pleas.

verses.summary: The break. The verb is now perfect, He has heard, and the phrase from verse 2 returns intact. That repetition is the only marker the psalm gives that anything changed.

stichs.en: The LORD is my strength and my shield;
in Him my heart trusted and I was helped.
My heart exults, and with my song I will thank Him.

verses.summary: Two clauses about the heart, one on each side of the help: the heart trusted, then the heart exults. The order matters, because the trust is not payment for the rescue.

stichs.en: The LORD is strength for them,
and a stronghold of deliverance for His anointed is He.

verses.summary: The private psalm goes public. The speaker stops being the subject, and strength now belongs to a group and to the anointed king.

stichs.en: Save Your people,
and bless Your inheritance;
shepherd them and carry them for ever.

verses.summary: Four imperatives for the nation, closing on a verb that belongs to shepherds. The final request is not rescue but being carried, with no end date attached.

pardes.body: A plea in verses 1 to 5 and a thanksgiving in verses 6 to 9, joined with no seam. The plea has three moves: do not be silent, do not sweep me up with the wicked, give them what they built. The thanksgiving has two: He heard me, and then, abruptly, save the whole people. What joins them is a word, not a logic. {{2.2}} in the plea comes back as {{6.5}} in the thanksgiving, the same noun for pleas, and the voice that asked to be heard is now said to have been heard. Nothing in the psalm describes a rescue. The change of tense is the entire event.

The sharpest move here is a repeated phrase. Verse 4 asks that the wicked be paid according to {{4.5}}, the work of their hands, and verse 5 convicts them for paying no attention to {{5.7}}, the work of His hands. One noun, two owners, and the whole justification of the sentence sits in that repetition. Verse 8 carries a textual crux: the Masoretic text has {{8.2}}, for them, with no clear antecedent in the line, and translations split between for them and for His people, a difference of a single letter. The choice decides whether the psalm turns communal at verse 8 or only at verse 9. And {{1.14}} is not a specific hole in the ground, it is the standard idiom for the grave across the Psalter.

Verse 4 is the verse readers flinch at, and the traditional handling of it is not to soften the request but to bound it. Nothing is asked for beyond measure: their deed, their doings, the work of their own hands, what they have earned, four statements of the same limit and none of them asking for more than was made. Verse 9 does something else with the discomfort. A psalm that spent five verses on one man's fear ends with four imperatives for a whole people, and the last of them, {{9.6}}, is the shepherd's verb, the one Psalm 23 opens with. The prayer that enemies be repaid and the prayer that a nation be carried are put in the same mouth, and the psalm makes no attempt to reconcile them.

The two nouns of verse 7 are read as a pair rather than a doubling: strength is what holds a person up from inside, the shield is what stands between him and what is outside, and both are named before the heart is allowed to move from trust to exultation. {{2.8}} in verse 2 is the innermost room of the sanctuary, the point with nothing further behind it, and hands lifted toward it are the standard image for raising what is below back toward its root. The closing verb belongs to the same reading: what can no longer walk is not abandoned but carried, and the psalm ends on the word for without limit in time.
